full_judgment:
20. In the case of Padam Prashad V. Emprror, AIR 1929 Cal. 617 (SB), it has been held that section 80 of the Evidence Act does not deal with the question of admissibility of the documents referred to therein but simply dispenses with the necessity of their formal proof by raising the presumption that everything in connection with them has been legally and correctly done. 

 21. In the case of Emperor V. Lalji Rai, AIR 1936 (Patna) 11, it was argued that the statements made under Ss. 164 and 512 Cr.P.C. were inadmissible in evidence inasmuch as the Magistrate who recorded those statements was not examined and therefore the statements were not duly proved. Repelling this contention it was held that where the statements of witnesses have been recorded under Ss. 164 and 512 Cr.P.C. a presumption of genuineness attaches to these statements under section 80 of the Evidence Act and the Magistrate recording the statements need not be examined in order to corroborate them. 

 22. The same conclusion has been arrived at in the case of Anwar Hussain Talukdar V. Province of East Pakistan, 12 DLR (Dhaka) 615. Same is the view taken by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in the case of Ismail Sarkar V. State, 33 DLR 320, where it has been held that section 80 of the Evidence Act dispenses with the necessity of formal proof of statements recorded under section 164 Cr.P.C. as there is a presumption that such a statement was genuinely recorded by the Magistrate.
